42863871.bottom_line: In a meta-analysis of 4 randomized trials (2,651 patients) with STEMI and multivessel disease, immediate complete revascularization was associated with higher 1-year all-cause mortality than a staged strategy (HR 1.50; 95% CI 1.02-2.21; P = 0.04), a statistically fragile signal that argues against routine immediate nonculprit PCI.
42863871.design: Frequentist pairwise random-effects meta-analysis of multicenter randomized controlled trials; protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251124207).
42863871.population: Patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel disease enrolled in multicenter RCTs; 4 trials comprising 2,651 patients. Trials required exclusive use of second-generation or newer drug-eluting stents and follow-up of at least 1 year.
42863871.intervention: Immediate complete revascularization, with nonculprit lesion PCI performed during the index procedure.
42863871.comparison: Staged complete revascularization, with nonculprit lesion PCI performed at a later time.
42863871.outcomes: Primary outcome was all-cause mortality: higher with immediate complete revascularization (HR 1.50; 95% CI 1.02-2.21; P = 0.04; prediction interval 0.80-2.81; I2 = 0%; tau2 = 0). Secondary outcomes were myocardial infarction, cardiac death and unplanned revascularization.
key_results: All-cause death at 1 year: HR 1.50 (95% CI 1.02-2.21; P = 0.04; prediction interval 0.80-2.81; I2 = 0%; tau2 = 0) with immediate versus staged complete revascularization.

Recurrent MI using protocol-specified definitions that included procedural MI: HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.36-0.94; P = 0.02; prediction interval 0.22-1.54; I2 = 0%; tau2 = 0.034), favouring immediate revascularization.
Spontaneous MI: HR 0.91 (95% CI 0.55-1.48; P = 0.90; prediction interval 0.41-2.00; I2 = 0%; tau2 = 0.00), no difference.
Cardiac death and unplanned revascularization were comparable between strategies (effect estimates not reported in the abstract).
Statistical heterogeneity was absent for the mortality endpoint (I2 = 0%), but the prediction interval crossed 1.0 (0.80-2.81).
strengths: Restricted to multicenter randomized trials, so the comparison of timing is based on randomized evidence rather than registry data.
Prespecified inclusion criteria requiring contemporary second-generation or newer drug-eluting stents and at least 1 year of follow-up, improving applicability to current practice.
Protocol registered prospectively on PROSPERO and analysed with random-effects models reporting prediction intervals as well as confidence intervals.
No statistical heterogeneity for the mortality and MI endpoints (I2 = 0%), suggesting consistency of direction across the 4 trials.
Directly addresses a decision clinicians face in every STEMI patient with multivessel disease.
limitations: Only 4 trials and 2,651 patients, with a relatively low number of deaths; the authors themselves describe the mortality finding as statistically fragile.
The mortality confidence interval barely excludes 1.0 (1.02-2.21) and the prediction interval (0.80-2.81) includes no effect, so a future trial could show no harm.

All-cause mortality was not the primary endpoint of the contributing trials, raising the possibility of a chance finding; cardiac death showed no difference, which is biologically discordant with an all-cause mortality excess.
Trial-level (not patient-level) HRs were pooled, preventing adjustment for baseline differences or analysis of subgroups such as shock, lesion complexity or timing of the staged procedure.
The apparent MI benefit of immediate revascularization depended on definitions including procedural MI and disappeared for spontaneous MI, so the endpoint advantage may be largely definitional.
Staging intervals, nonculprit assessment methods and crossover rates across the included trials are not reported in the abstract, and funding was not reported.
42863871.practice_implications: These pooled randomized data do not support routinely completing nonculprit PCI during the index STEMI procedure. For haemodynamically stable patients, deferring nonculprit revascularization to a staged procedure remains the safer default, while accepting that the mortality signal rests on few events and that the apparent reduction in recurrent MI with immediate treatment is driven by periprocedural events. Immediate treatment may still be reasonable for selected patients with ongoing ischaemia or instability, where the trials provide little guidance.

42866879.bottom_line: In this prespecified bleeding analysis of OCEANIC-STROKE (12,254 participants), adding the factor XIa inhibitor asundexian to antiplatelet therapy after noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA did not significantly increase major bleeding (1.9% vs 1.7%; csHR 1.10 [95% CI, 0.85-1.44]; P=0.46), but lower gastrointestinal bleeding was more frequent (1.7% vs 1.0%; csHR 1.75 [95% CI, 1.27-2.41]).
42866879.design: Prespecified safety/bleeding analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (OCEANIC-STROKE; NCT05686070), with while-on-treatment analyses including events through 2 days after the last dose and death and permanent discontinuation handled as competing risks.
42866879.population: Safety population of 12,254 participants with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack who received at least 1 dose of study drug (asundexian n=6,124; placebo n=6,130).
42866879.intervention: Asundexian added to background antiplatelet therapy (dose not reported in the abstract).
42866879.comparison: Placebo added to background antiplatelet therapy.
42866879.outcomes: Bleeding categorized by International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria as major, clinically relevant nonmajor (CRNM), or minor. Major bleeding: 117 (1.9%) with asundexian vs 107 (1.7%) with placebo (csHR 1.10 [95% CI, 0.85-1.44]; P=0.46). Major or CRNM bleeding: 339 (5.5%) vs 307 (5.0%) (csHR 1.12 [95% CI, 0.96-1.30]; P=0.16). Any bleeding: 763 (12.5%) vs 752 (12.3%) (csHR 1.02 [95% CI, 0.93-1.13]; P=0.65).
key_results: Major bleeding: 117 (1.9%) asundexian vs 107 (1.7%) placebo; csHR 1.10 (95% CI, 0.85-1.44); P=0.46.
Major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding: 339 (5.5%) vs 307 (5.0%); csHR 1.12 (95% CI, 0.96-1.30); P=0.16.
Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage: 41 (0.7%) with asundexian vs 36 (0.6%) with placebo (comparative effect estimate not reported).

Any gastrointestinal bleeding: 186 (3.0%) vs 147 (2.4%); csHR 1.28 (95% CI, 1.03-1.59). Lower gastrointestinal bleeding: 102 (1.7%) vs 59 (1.0%); csHR 1.75 (95% CI, 1.27-2.41), primarily rectal bleeding.
Treatment effects on major and major or CRNM bleeding were consistent across prespecified subgroups, including planned dual antiplatelet therapy.
Procedure-related bleeding and mucosal bleeding did not differ significantly (effect estimates not reported).
strengths: Large randomized, placebo-controlled safety population (12,254 participants) with balanced group sizes, so bleeding comparisons are not confounded by indication.
Bleeding adjudicated using standard ISTH categories, with reporting by severity and by anatomical site rather than a single composite.
While-on-treatment analysis with death and permanent discontinuation treated as competing risks, which is the appropriate framework for drug-attributable bleeding.
Prespecified subgroup analyses, including the clinically important subgroup receiving planned dual antiplatelet therapy, showed consistency.
Directly addresses the key clinical question for factor XIa inhibition: whether the ischemic benefit seen in the parent trial comes at a bleeding cost.
limitations: Secondary safety analysis of a completed trial, so the site-specific and subgroup comparisons are exploratory and not adjusted for multiplicity; the lower gastrointestinal bleeding finding could reflect chance among many comparisons.

Absolute event numbers for the more severe endpoints are modest (117 vs 107 major bleeds; 41 vs 36 symptomatic intracranial hemorrhages), so the confidence interval for major bleeding (0.85-1.44) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful 44% relative increase.
Intracranial hemorrhage was reported descriptively without a hazard ratio or P value, limiting interpretation of the endpoint cardiologists and neurologists most fear.
Asundexian dose, duration of exposure, follow-up time and background antiplatelet regimens are not reported in the abstract.
While-on-treatment censoring 2 days after the last dose excludes later events and may understate bleeding in patients who discontinue.
Efficacy outcomes are not re-reported here, so net clinical benefit cannot be computed from this analysis alone; funding and sponsor role are not reported in the abstract.
42866879.practice_implications: Asundexian is not yet approved, but these data support the central premise of factor XIa inhibition: meaningful antithrombotic effect without the expected excess in major or intracranial bleeding when added to antiplatelet therapy after noncardioembolic stroke. The signal for lower gastrointestinal bleeding, mostly rectal, is the practical caveat and suggests that if the drug reaches clinic, patients with prior gastrointestinal bleeding or anorectal pathology will warrant closer counselling and a low threshold to investigate new rectal bleeding rather than attribute it to haemorrhoids.

42862588.bottom_line: Using US transplant registry data (training n=21,859; validation n=7,897; test n=8,256), a continuous medical urgency score (US-CRS) built from 5 laboratory values and 4 support devices discriminated 6-week mortality without transplant far better than the current 6-status system (mean time-dependent AUC 0.807 vs 0.693) and, in simulation, would place sicker candidates at the top of the match run (observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate 15.7% [95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%] vs 11.2% [95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%]).
42862588.design: Registry-based observational development and validation study with chronologically split training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024) and test (2024-2025) datasets, a marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant, comparison of 8 candidate models in held-out data, and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering.
42862588.population: All adult (aged 18 years or older) US heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025: training n=21,859, validation n=7,897, test n=8,256 (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). Match-run analysis covered 45,530 donor hearts.
42862588.intervention: Ranking of candidates by the US Candidate Risk Score (US-CRS), a continuous medical urgency score comprising 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support).
42862588.comparison: The current 6-status, therapy-based US donor heart allocation system.
42862588.outcomes: Six-week mortality without transplant, assessed by weighted time-dependent AUC and calibration by status. In test-set cross-sections of candidates waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693). In the match-run simulation, observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run rose from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under US-CRS.
key_results: Mean time-dependent AUC for 6-week mortality without transplant: 0.807 with US-CRS vs 0.693 with the current 6-status system in test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date.
US-CRS showed acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception - the group the current system handles worst.
The selected model used 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable LVAD, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, advanced mechanical circulatory support).
Match-run simulation across 45,530 donor hearts: 67% of transplant recipients moved down in rank order under a US-CRS-based policy.

Observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality of the first candidate on the match run: 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under US-CRS vs 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system, indicating the score puts higher-risk candidates first.
Eight candidate models were compared in held-out data before the final score was chosen.
strengths: National registry coverage of all adult US candidates over 2019-2025, so the development population is the actual target population for the policy.
Chronological rather than random data splitting, with a test set (2024-2025) later than the development data, which tests robustness to practice drift and to the 2018 allocation-policy era.
A marginal structural model appropriately handles the time-varying nature of therapy and the competing event of transplant, rather than modelling mortality at listing only.
Evaluation goes beyond discrimination to calibration by status and to a concrete match-run simulation of 45,530 donor hearts, translating a statistical model into policy consequences.
Built from objective laboratory values and device support rather than therapy-based tiers, directly targeting the gaming and exception-request problems of the current 6-status system.
Large absolute improvement in discrimination (AUC 0.807 vs 0.693) that is unlikely to be explained by overfitting given held-out testing.
limitations: Observational registry study: the benefit is demonstrated as better risk ranking, not as improved waitlist or post-transplant survival, which no simulation can establish.

Six-week mortality without transplant is a surrogate for the real objective of maximizing survival benefit; prioritizing the sickest candidates may not maximize post-transplant survival or total life-years, and post-transplant outcomes were not modelled.

Registry data are subject to missing and misreported laboratory values and to centre-level variation in practice; the score's inputs (e.g. device use) remain partly under centre control and could themselves be gamed.
The match-run simulation assumes unchanged candidate listing and acceptance behaviour, which would almost certainly change under a new policy.

Score performance in important subgroups (women, congenital heart disease, amyloidosis, retransplant, candidates on durable LVAD support) and the identity of the 5 laboratory values are not reported in the abstract.
Calibration was assessed by current status categories, and the trade-off of 67% of recipients moving down in rank order - including which groups lose priority - is not quantified in the abstract.
Funding and sponsor role are not reported.
42862588.practice_implications: For clinicians who list patients for heart transplantation, this is the evidence base behind the expected move from the 6-status tiers to a continuous US-CRS-based urgency score. Practically, allocation priority would shift toward objective physiology (laboratory values) interacting with the type of mechanical support, reducing the value of status-by-exception requests and of therapy choices made to secure a tier. Listing practice, documentation of laboratory data and the timing of device escalation would all become more consequential, while candidates currently advantaged by therapy-based tiering - 67% of recipients moved down in rank in simulation - may wait longer.

42872914.bottom_line: In 584 adults with septic shock undergoing surgical source control at 39 Chinese hospitals, adding intraoperative dobutamine (up to 5 ug/kg/min) to norepinephrine reduced new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days from 34.7% (102/294) to 22.8% (66/290) (adjusted risk ratio 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]), with more tachycardia and no difference in 9 of 11 secondary outcomes.
42872914.design: Randomized, open-label clinical trial at 39 tertiary hospitals in China, enrolling June 2024 to August 2025 with follow-up ending 15 November 2025 (NCT06462313).
42872914.population: 584 adults with septic shock undergoing surgical source control (median [IQR] age 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] female); 290 assigned to dobutamine plus norepinephrine and 294 to norepinephrine alone.
42872914.intervention: Intraoperative intravenous dobutamine infusion up to 5 ug/kg/min combined with norepinephrine.
42872914.outcomes: Primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery by KDIGO criteria: 22.8% (66/290) with dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) with norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). There were 11 secondary outcomes, including SOFA score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention.
key_results: Primary outcome (new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days): 22.8% (66/290) vs 34.7% (102/294); adjusted risk ratio 0.64 (95% CI, 0.49-0.83).
Stage 2 AKI: 4.8% vs 9.9%; adjusted risk ratio 0.48 (95% CI, 0.26-0.88). Stage 3 AKI: 7.9% vs 13.6%; adjusted risk ratio 0.56 (95% CI, 0.35-0.91).
SOFA score on postoperative day 1: adjusted difference -0.53 (95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07), favouring dobutamine plus norepinephrine.
Urine output 1 hour after intervention: adjusted difference 0.55 (95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07) mL/kg/h, higher with dobutamine plus norepinephrine.
No significant differences in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes.
Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently with dobutamine plus norepinephrine (rates and effect estimate not reported).
Mortality was not reported among the results in the abstract.
strengths: Randomized design addressing a question previously supported only by very low-certainty evidence despite a guideline recommendation for dobutamine in septic shock with cardiac dysfunction.
Multicentre (39 tertiary hospitals), giving reasonable spread of practice within the host country.
Clinically meaningful, objectively defined primary outcome using standard KDIGO criteria, with a large absolute reduction (22.8% vs 34.7%).
Internally consistent effect across AKI severity, with reductions in both stage 2 (ARR 0.48) and stage 3 (ARR 0.56) injury rather than only mild creatinine shifts.
Supportive physiological signals in the same direction (lower day 1 SOFA, higher early urine output).
Prospectively registered with a prespecified primary outcome and a defined follow-up end date.
limitations: Open-label with no placebo infusion, so decisions about fluids, vasopressors, nephrotoxins and renal replacement therapy could have been influenced by knowledge of allocation - a major concern for a creatinine- and urine-output-based endpoint.
The primary outcome is AKI within 7 days rather than a patient-important outcome; mortality, dialysis dependence and length of stay are not reported in the abstract.

Nine of 11 secondary outcomes showed no difference, and the two positive ones (day 1 SOFA, 1-hour urine output) have confidence intervals that approach the null, with no apparent correction for multiplicity.
Conducted entirely in Chinese tertiary hospitals; baseline AKI rates of 34.7% in the control arm are high, so absolute benefit may not transfer to settings with different practice.
Reported effects are adjusted risk ratios with no unadjusted figures or P values given, and the adjustment model is not described in the abstract.

Tachycardia was more frequent but arrhythmia, myocardial injury and other dobutamine-specific harms are not quantified; whether patients had baseline cardiac dysfunction (the guideline indication) is not stated.
Follow-up limited to the early postoperative period; funding and sponsor role are not reported.
42872914.practice_implications: For cardiologists consulted on septic shock in the perioperative setting, this is the first randomized support for adding low-dose dobutamine to norepinephrine during surgical source control, with a substantial reduction in postoperative AKI including stage 2 and 3 injury. The open-label design and the absence of reported mortality or dialysis outcomes mean this should not yet be treated as a mandate; it is reasonable to consider low-dose dobutamine in septic shock patients with hypoperfusion going to the operating room, while monitoring for tachycardia and awaiting confirmation in blinded trials reporting patient-important endpoints.

42872757.bottom_line: In SUBCUT-HF II, an open-label UK trial of 172 patients hospitalized for heart failure and still requiring parenteral diuretics, early discharge on wearable-minipump subcutaneous furosemide gained 4.0 more days alive and out of hospital at 30 days (95% CI: 2.1-5.8; P < 0.001) and shortened index admission by 5.5 days (95% CI: 7.4-3.6; P < 0.001), at the cost of numerically more heart failure readmissions (14% vs 6%; OR 2.45 [95% CI: 0.81-7.43]).
42872757.design: Multicenter, open-label, randomized, active-controlled trial in the United Kingdom (SUBCUT-HF II; NCT05419115).
42872757.population: 172 patients hospitalized for heart failure who required ongoing parenteral diuretic therapy; 92 assigned to the early discharge strategy and 80 to usual care.
42872757.intervention: Early discharge strategy with pH-neutral subcutaneous furosemide delivered by a wearable, patient-operated minipump, plus postdischarge review every 3 days while receiving subcutaneous furosemide.
42872757.comparison: Usual inpatient care with continued conventional parenteral diuretic therapy. Both groups had a 2-week clinic review.
42872757.outcomes: Primary outcome was days alive and out of hospital (DAOH) at 30 days after randomization: 4.0 more DAOH with early discharge (95% CI: 2.1-5.8 days; P < 0.001).
key_results: Primary outcome, DAOH at 30 days: 4.0 days more with the early discharge strategy (95% CI: 2.1-5.8 days; P < 0.001).
Index hospitalization shorter by a mean of 5.5 days (95% CI: 7.4-3.6 days; P < 0.001).
DAOH benefit sustained at 60 days: difference 4.2 days (95% CI: 0.9-7.6 days).
Heart failure readmissions: 13 (14%) in the early discharge group vs 5 (6%) with usual care; OR 2.45 (95% CI: 0.81-7.43).
Serious adverse events: 25% with early discharge vs 23% with usual care.
Device-related problems occurred with 3% of minipump placements, none serious.
strengths: Randomized and multicenter, testing a complete care strategy rather than a drug, which is how the intervention would be used in practice.
DAOH is a patient-centred primary endpoint that captures both survival and hospital burden, and the benefit was large relative to its confidence interval (4.0 days, 95% CI 2.1-5.8).
Benefit persisted at 60 days (4.2 days, 95% CI 0.9-7.6), so the gain was not merely a shifted admission.
Enrolled the clinically relevant population - patients still requiring parenteral diuretics - rather than patients already ready for discharge.
Structured postdischarge safety net (review every 3 days) that is reproducible, with serious adverse events similar between arms (25% vs 23%) and few device problems (3%, none serious).
limitations: Small trial (172 patients; 92 vs 80) and open-label, with no blinding of patients, clinicians or outcome ascertainment; length of stay and discharge timing are investigator-determined and highly susceptible to performance bias.
Unequal group sizes (92 vs 80) are unexplained in the abstract and raise questions about the randomization procedure.
DAOH is partly a direct consequence of the intervention itself (earlier discharge), so a positive result is close to inevitable by design; it does not establish clinical benefit.

Heart failure readmissions were more than twice as frequent with early discharge (14% vs 6%); the trial was underpowered for this outcome (OR 2.45, 95% CI 0.81-7.43) and cannot exclude meaningful harm.
No reported effect on mortality, renal function, electrolytes, symptoms or quality of life in the abstract, and no cost-effectiveness data despite the economic rationale.
Single-country (UK) trial with intensive 3-day review, requiring both the pH-neutral subcutaneous furosemide formulation and a community follow-up infrastructure that many systems lack.
Follow-up limited to 60 days; funding and sponsor role are not reported.
42872757.practice_implications: For selected, otherwise stable patients whose only reason to remain in hospital is ongoing parenteral diuresis, subcutaneous furosemide via a wearable minipump with structured 3-day review can plausibly free several hospital days without an excess of serious adverse events. The trial is small, open-label and shows a doubling of heart failure readmissions that it cannot rule out as real, so this is best viewed as a promising, resource-dependent pathway for carefully chosen patients and systems that can guarantee close follow-up, rather than an established standard.

42861574.bottom_line: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 37 studies (n = 1,298,291), physical activity was associated with 22% lower odds of atrial fibrillation in the general population (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.68, 0.89) while athlete status was associated with substantially higher odds (OR 2.74; 95% CI 1.72, 4.39); spline modelling placed the greatest benefit at 26 MET-hr/wk and a reversal to increased odds beyond 78 MET-hr/wk, roughly 6-7 hours per week of endurance training.
42861574.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with weighted random-effects pooling and a weighted restricted cubic spline dose-response model of logarithmic odds; four databases searched from January 1990 to June 2025.
42861574.population: 37 included studies comprising 1,298,291 individuals, from general populations through to athletes; the dose-response analysis used 26 studies (n = 1,022,790).
42861574.intervention: Physical activity exposure, standardised across studies to metabolic equivalent of task hours per week (MET-hr/wk), including athlete status as a separate exposure category.
42861574.comparison: Sedentary control groups within each included study.
42861574.outcomes: Atrial fibrillation incidence or prevalence, expressed as pooled odds ratios. In the general population, physical activity was associated with a 22% reduction in odds of AF (22 studies; OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.68, 0.89). Athlete status was associated with increased odds of AF (15 studies; OR 2.74; 95% CI 1.72, 4.39). P values were not reported.
key_results: General population: physical activity associated with 22% lower odds of atrial fibrillation (22 studies; OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.68, 0.89).
Athlete status: higher odds of atrial fibrillation (15 studies; OR 2.74; 95% CI 1.72, 4.39).
Dose-response (26 studies; n = 1,022,790): greatest reduction in odds of AF at 26 MET-hr/wk of physical activity.
Doses beyond 78 MET-hr/wk were associated with increased odds of AF, described by the authors as the equivalent of 6-7 hours per week of endurance training.
The overall relationship was U-shaped across the full continuum of exposure.
strengths: Very large pooled sample (1,298,291 individuals across 37 studies), giving precision at both ends of the exposure range.
Exposures standardised to MET-hr/wk, allowing heterogeneous activity measures to be placed on one quantitative scale and producing an actionable numeric threshold.
Spline modelling of the full continuum rather than category comparisons, which is the only way to locate the point at which the curve reverses.
Broad search across four databases over a 35-year window, with athletes analysed separately from general populations.
Addresses a question patients ask directly - how much endurance exercise is too much - and translates the threshold into hours of training per week.
limitations: Pooling of observational studies only: the associations cannot establish that high exercise volume causes atrial fibrillation, and residual confounding (height, body size, alcohol, sleep apnoea, hypertension) is likely.
Both incidence and prevalence studies were combined and results are reported as odds ratios, mixing study designs and inviting bias in the pooled estimate.

Detection bias is a major concern at the extremes: athletes are more monitored and more symptom-aware, and AF ascertainment methods are likely to differ between athlete cohorts and general populations.

Physical activity is overwhelmingly self-reported in epidemiological cohorts, so the MET-hr/wk conversion carries substantial measurement error, and the 26 and 78 MET-hr/wk thresholds are modelled point estimates presented without confidence intervals.
Heterogeneity statistics (I2), P values, publication-bias assessment, risk-of-bias ratings and whether the review was prospectively registered are not reported in the abstract.
The athlete estimate is imprecise (95% CI 1.72, 4.39) and 'athlete' is a heterogeneous category spanning very different sports, sexes, ages and training histories.
Funding is not reported.
42861574.practice_implications: This supports the standard advice that regular moderate activity protects against atrial fibrillation, and provides a number to use in conversation: benefit appears maximal around 26 MET-hr/wk, with a signal of increased AF odds beyond roughly 78 MET-hr/wk or 6-7 hours per week of endurance training. Because the evidence is observational and vulnerable to detection bias, it should temper rather than forbid high-volume training: a reason to discuss AF risk, symptoms and modifiable co-factors such as alcohol with endurance athletes, and reassurance that nothing here argues against recommending ordinary exercise volumes to patients at risk of AF.

42888496.bottom_line: In a meta-analysis of 31 studies (26,948 dyspneic emergency department patients), NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or below ruled out acute heart failure with 97.9% (96.9-98.5) sensitivity and a 97.0% (96.5-97.4) negative predictive value, while age-dependent rule-in thresholds (450, 900 and 1,800 ng/L for ages <50, 50-75 and 75+ years) outperformed fixed thresholds (AUC 0.84 [0.83-0.85] vs 0.73 [0.69-0.77]); performance fell in chronic kidney disease (AUC 0.77 [0.75-0.78]).
42888496.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies published up to 28 August 2025.
42888496.population: 31 studies comprising 26,948 patients presenting to the emergency department with dyspnoea. Subgroup analyses included age-dependent thresholds in 14,410 patients, chronic kidney disease in 2,271 patients and obesity (body mass index 30 or above) in 3,562 patients.
42888496.intervention: NT-proBNP measurement interpreted against fixed thresholds (including 300 ng/L or below for rule-out) and against age-dependent thresholds of 450 ng/L or above for patients aged under 50 years, 900 ng/L or above for ages 50-75 years, and 1,800 ng/L or above for ages 75 years and over.
42888496.comparison: Reference standard diagnosis of acute heart failure as adjudicated in each included study; fixed versus age-dependent threshold strategies were compared against one another.
42888496.outcomes: Diagnostic accuracy (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, negative predictive value). Rule-out threshold 300 ng/L or below: AUC 0.73 (0.69-0.77), sensitivity 97.9% (96.9-98.5), specificity 46.2% (36.4-56.2), negative predictive value 97.0% (96.5-97.4). Age-dependent thresholds: AUC 0.84 (0.83-0.85), sensitivity 85.9% (85.0-86.7), specificity 82.0% (81.2-82.9). P values were not reported.
key_results: Rule-out with NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or below: AUC 0.73 (0.69-0.77), sensitivity 97.9% (96.9-98.5), specificity 46.2% (36.4-56.2), negative predictive value 97.0% (96.5-97.4).

Age-dependent thresholds (450 ng/L if aged <50 years, 900 ng/L if 50-75 years, 1,800 ng/L if 75 years or over), assessed in 14,410 patients: AUC 0.84 (0.83-0.85), sensitivity 85.9% (85.0-86.7), specificity 82.0% (81.2-82.9).
Chronic kidney disease (n = 2,271): all fixed thresholds gave AUC below 0.80; age-dependent thresholds gave AUC 0.77 (0.75-0.78) with specificity only 62.6% (59.4-65.7).
Obesity with body mass index 30 or above (n = 3,562, age-dependent thresholds only): AUC 0.82 (0.81-0.84), sensitivity 81.2% (79.2-83.1), broadly comparable to the overall population.
The authors conclude that 300 ng/L or below is an excellent rule-out threshold while age-dependent thresholds are superior for ruling in acute heart failure.
strengths: Large pooled diagnostic dataset (31 studies, 26,948 patients) addressing the exact decision made at the front door in dyspnoea.
Evaluates both rule-out and rule-in strategies rather than a single cut-point, and reports sensitivity, specificity, AUC and negative predictive value with confidence intervals.
Prespecified clinically important subgroups (chronic kidney disease, obesity) in which natriuretic peptide interpretation is known to be problematic.
Directly validates the age-stratified thresholds already embedded in guidelines, giving quantitative support for a strategy many clinicians already use.
Confirms the high negative predictive value (97.0%) that underpins safe discharge decisions in low-probability patients.
Recent search date (August 2025), so contemporary assays and practice are represented.
limitations: Meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies with heterogeneous reference standards for acute heart failure adjudication, which is itself imperfect and often informed by the biomarker under test (incorporation bias).

Pooled sensitivity and specificity depend heavily on disease prevalence and spectrum in the contributing emergency departments, so the reported negative predictive value will not transfer to settings with very different pretest probability.
Heterogeneity statistics (I2), risk-of-bias assessment (for example QUADAS-2), publication-bias testing and whether the review was prospectively registered are not reported in the abstract.

Subgroup evidence is thin: only 2,271 patients with chronic kidney disease and 3,562 with obesity, with obesity assessed only for age-dependent thresholds and no renal-function-specific thresholds tested.
Specificity of the 300 ng/L rule-out threshold is poor (46.2%), so this cut-point alone leaves a large indeterminate group, and the intermediate 'grey zone' is not characterised.

Confidence intervals around some pooled estimates are implausibly narrow for aggregated diagnostic data, suggesting fixed-effect-like pooling or within-study correlation that may understate uncertainty.
Assay platforms, timing of sampling relative to presentation, and treatment before sampling are not described; P values and funding are not reported.
42888496.practice_implications: This supports current practice: use NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or below to rule out acute heart failure in the dyspneic emergency department patient, where the 97.0% negative predictive value makes an alternative diagnosis the safer working assumption, and use the age-stratified cut-points (450, 900 and 1,800 ng/L) rather than a single fixed rule-in value. The caution is renal dysfunction, where accuracy drops and specificity falls to about 63% - here a raised NT-proBNP should prompt imaging and clinical correlation rather than a diagnosis. Obesity, reassuringly, did not materially degrade performance of the age-dependent thresholds.

42876202.bottom_line: Across 56 chronic heart failure randomized trials (39 drug, 17 device), women made up only 27.0% (95% CI: 22.0% to 32.4%) of drug-trial and 25.3% (95% CI: 21.0% to 29.9%) of device-trial participants - 21.0% in HFrEF versus 49.6% in HFpEF trials (p < 0.001) - and pooled sex-interaction estimates hinted at a somewhat greater relative treatment benefit in women (drug trials: HR interaction 0.94 [95% CI 0.89-1.01], RR interaction 0.81 [95% CI 0.68-0.96]).
42876202.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials searched in PubMed-MEDLINE, using random-effects models with prespecified subgroup analyses of pooled sex-treatment interaction estimates.
42876202.population: 56 randomized controlled trials in chronic heart failure (39 drug trials, 17 device trials) that tested pharmacological or device-based interventions against a hard primary endpoint (mortality and hospitalization) and reported enrollment of women.
42876202.intervention: Female sex as the modifier of randomized pharmacological or device-based heart failure therapy; the analysis pooled trial-reported sex-specific treatment effects (HR or RR).
42876202.comparison: Male sex within the same trials; enrollment proportions were also compared between HFrEF and HFpEF trials and between drug and device trials.
42876202.outcomes: Proportion of women enrolled and pooled sex-treatment interaction on trial primary endpoints (mortality and hospitalization). Pooled women enrollment: 27.0% (95% CI: 22.0% to 32.4%) in drug trials and 25.3% (95% CI: 21.0% to 29.9%) in device trials. Pooled sex interaction in drug trials: 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-1.01) for trials reporting HR and 0.81 (95% CI 0.68-0.96) for those reporting RR.
key_results: Pooled proportion of women enrolled: 27.0% (95% CI: 22.0% to 32.4%) in drug trials and 25.3% (95% CI: 21.0% to 29.9%) in device trials.
Women were far more underrepresented in HFrEF than HFpEF trials: 21.0% vs 49.6% (p < 0.001).
Drug trials, pooled sex interaction: 0.94 (95% CI 0.89-1.01) among trials reporting hazard ratios and 0.81 (95% CI 0.68-0.96) among those reporting risk ratios, both directionally favouring women.
No interaction between HFrEF and HFpEF trials (HR: p = 0.44; RR: p = 0.95).
Pooled interaction estimate on event counts: 0.90 (95% CI 0.84-0.96).
Device trials, pooled sex interaction: 1.05 (95% CI 0.90-1.22) for trials reporting HR and 0.68 (95% CI 0.50-0.93) for those reporting RR.
strengths: Restricted to randomized trials with hard primary endpoints (mortality and hospitalization), so the treatment-effect comparisons rest on randomized evidence rather than observational data.
Covers a substantial body of evidence (56 trials) and separates drug from device interventions, which have different mechanisms of potential sex-related effect modification.
Quantifies the enrollment gap precisely and exposes the striking HFrEF versus HFpEF contrast (21.0% vs 49.6%), which localizes where the representation problem actually lies.
Uses interaction estimates rather than naive comparison of within-sex effect sizes, which is the methodologically correct approach to effect modification.
Prespecified subgroup analyses and random-effects pooling, with consistency checks across HR, RR and event-count metrics.
limitations: Meta-analysis of trial-level published subgroup data, not individual patient data, so the interaction estimates are vulnerable to reporting bias - only trials that published sex-specific effects could contribute.
Sex subgroup analyses within individual trials are typically underpowered and exploratory; pooling them does not overcome the fact that none was designed to detect sex-treatment interaction.

The headline drug-trial interaction is inconsistent across metrics: the HR-based estimate crosses unity (0.94; 95% CI 0.89-1.01) while the RR-based estimate does not (0.81; 95% CI 0.68-0.96), and the same discordance appears for devices (HR 1.05 vs RR 0.68), suggesting the finding is metric-dependent rather than robust.
Pooling heterogeneous interventions, eras, endpoints and follow-up durations into a single interaction estimate has questionable clinical interpretability.
Search limited to PubMed-MEDLINE, raising the possibility of missed trials; heterogeneity statistics (I2), risk-of-bias assessment and prospective registration are not reported in the abstract.
Lower enrollment of women partly reflects the true epidemiology of HFrEF rather than selection alone, and the analysis cannot separate recruitment bias from disease distribution.
No exploration of mechanisms (pharmacokinetics, dosing, body size, adherence) and no data on whether women received comparable doses; funding is not reported.
42876202.practice_implications: Nothing here changes how to treat an individual woman with heart failure, but two points are worth carrying into clinic. First, the evidence base for HFrEF therapy is drawn from cohorts only about one-fifth female, which should be acknowledged rather than ignored when extrapolating - though the interaction estimates give no reason to expect less benefit in women, if anything the opposite. Second, the signal of possibly greater relative benefit, taken with known sex differences in drug exposure at a given dose, reinforces that women should be titrated to guideline-directed target doses rather than left at lower doses, and strengthens the case for trials powered to examine sex-specific dosing and response.

42862105.bottom_line: In 56,362 patients aged 45 years or older undergoing non-cardiac surgery at two university hospitals, established preoperative statin therapy was associated with lower 365-day mortality (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.73-0.90; absolute risk difference -1.2 percentage points; number needed to treat 83) in a dose-dependent fashion (high-intensity HR 0.71 [95% CI 0.60-0.83]; low/intermediate-intensity HR 0.84 [95% CI 0.74-0.96]), while the 30-day association was directionally similar but not significant (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.57-1.07).
42862105.design: Retrospective observational cohort study (2016-2023) at two university hospitals, using inverse probability of treatment weighting with random forest-estimated propensity scores targeting the average treatment effect in the treated, with associations estimated by weighted Cox regression.
42862105.population: 56,362 patients aged 45 years or older undergoing non-cardiac surgery at two university hospitals between 2016 and 2023. Overall, 372 patients (0.6%) died within 30 days and 3,735 (6.6%) within 365 days.
42862105.intervention: Established preoperative statin exposure, assessed as status (any vs none), intensity (high vs low/intermediate) and regimen (high vs low/intermediate vs none).
42862105.outcomes: Primary outcomes were 30- and 365-day mortality. Statin therapy was associated with a non-significant reduction in 30-day mortality (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.57-1.07) and with lower 365-day mortality (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.73-0.90; absolute risk difference -1.2 percentage points; number needed to treat 83). P values were not reported.
key_results: 30-day mortality: HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.57-1.07) - directionally consistent but not statistically significant.
365-day mortality: HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.73-0.90), absolute risk difference -1.2 percentage points, number needed to treat 83.
Dose-response versus no statin at 365 days: high-intensity therapy HR 0.71 (95% CI 0.60-0.83) with absolute risk difference -2.3 points; low/intermediate-intensity HR 0.84 (95% CI 0.74-0.96).
Event numbers: 372 deaths (0.6%) at 30 days and 3,735 deaths (6.6%) at 365 days.
All covariates were balanced after weighting, and findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
strengths: Large cohort (56,362 patients) with enough 1-year deaths (3,735) to estimate the long-term association precisely.
Addresses a question that randomized evidence cannot currently answer, since trials of de novo perioperative statin initiation were discredited by research misconduct.

Modern causal-inference approach: inverse probability of treatment weighting with machine-learning (random forest) propensity scores targeting the average treatment effect in the treated, with documented covariate balance after weighting.
Internally coherent dose-response gradient (high-intensity HR 0.71 vs low/intermediate HR 0.84), which strengthens the case for a real biological effect rather than pure confounding.
Reports absolute risk differences and a number needed to treat alongside hazard ratios, making the magnitude interpretable.
Findings stated to be consistent across sensitivity analyses.
limitations: Observational design: statin users are systematically different from non-users, and the central threat here is healthy-user and healthy-adherer bias, which propensity weighting on measured covariates cannot remove.

Confounding by indication runs in both directions - statin users have more atherosclerotic disease but are also more engaged with medical care - so residual confounding is likely and the direction unpredictable.

Exposure was defined by preoperative prescription status; actual perioperative continuation, adherence, duration of prior therapy, LDL cholesterol achieved and postoperative resumption are not reported.

A survival benefit at 365 days without a significant 30-day effect is more consistent with the known long-term benefit of statins in patients with vascular disease than with a specific perioperative mechanism; the window of attribution is unclear.
Two university hospitals only, so case mix, surgical practice and prescribing patterns may not generalise.

Composite 'morbidity' outcomes promised in the title are not reported in the abstract, nor are cause-specific mortality, myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, or statin-related harms such as myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
No P values are given, the covariate set used for weighting is not described, and funding is not reported.
The authors themselves call for randomized confirmation; until then the number needed to treat of 83 should not be read as a causal estimate.
42862105.practice_implications: This does not justify starting a statin solely to cover an operation, but it adds weight to the practical rule of not stopping one. For patients already on statin therapy who are scheduled for non-cardiac surgery, the data support continuing it through the perioperative period - and, where indicated on standard cardiovascular grounds, continuing at high intensity rather than de-escalating. The absence of a convincing 30-day signal suggests the benefit observed is largely the ordinary long-term benefit of statin therapy in a high-risk surgical population, which is itself a reason to use the surgical episode as an opportunity to review and optimise lipid-lowering treatment.

42872886.bottom_line: Among 237,729 UK Biobank participants of European ancestry free of ASCVD at baseline and followed for a median of 14.1 years, Lp(a) at or above the ESC/EAS 2025 threshold of 105 nmol/L was associated with a 50% higher rate of coronary, peripheral and carotid revascularization (Andersen-Gill HR 1.50, 1.42-1.60) and a 55% higher procedure rate (IRR 1.55, 1.45-1.65), with the association strongest for the first procedure (HR 1.48, 1.40-1.56) and attenuating for subsequent ones.
42872886.design: Observational prospective cohort analysis of UK Biobank using recurrent-event methodology: the Andersen-Gill model, negative binomial regression and the Prentice-Williams-Peterson gap-time model, rather than time-to-first-event analysis alone.
42872886.population: 237,729 UK Biobank participants of European ancestry, free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease at baseline, followed for a median of 14.1 years; 10,731 revascularization procedures occurred.
42872886.intervention: Elevated lipoprotein(a), analysed dichotomously at the ESC/EAS 2025 threshold of 105 nmol/L and continuously per 50 nmol/L increment.
42872886.outcomes: Primary outcome was the total number of coronary, peripheral and carotid revascularization procedures per person. Lp(a) 105 nmol/L or above was associated with a higher revascularization rate (Andersen-Gill HR 1.50, 1.42-1.60) and a 55% higher procedure rate by negative binomial regression (IRR 1.55, 1.45-1.65). P values were not reported.
key_results: Andersen-Gill model: HR 1.50 (1.42-1.60) for revascularization rate with Lp(a) 105 nmol/L or above.
Negative binomial regression: IRR 1.55 (1.45-1.65), a 55% higher rate of revascularization procedures during follow-up.
Proportion undergoing at least 1 procedure: 4.36% with Lp(a) 105 nmol/L or above vs 2.96% below; at least 2 procedures 1.53% vs 0.95%; at least 3 procedures 0.36% vs 0.18%.
Prentice-Williams-Peterson gap-time analysis by event order: first procedure HR 1.48 (1.40-1.56), second HR 1.28 (1.09-1.50), third HR 1.23 (0.94-1.62, non-significant).
Findings were consistent across coronary and peripheral territories; the carotid analysis was inconclusive owing to limited statistical power.
10,731 revascularization procedures occurred overall in 237,729 participants.
strengths: Very large primary prevention cohort (237,729 participants) with long median follow-up of 14.1 years and a substantial number of events (10,731 procedures), giving narrow confidence intervals.
Recurrent-event methods capture total procedural burden rather than only the first event, which is the more complete way to quantify the consequences of a lifelong, genetically determined exposure.
Three complementary models (Andersen-Gill, negative binomial, Prentice-Williams-Peterson) gave concordant estimates, arguing against a methodological artefact.
Uses the current ESC/EAS 2025 threshold of 105 nmol/L and also models Lp(a) continuously, making results directly interpretable against contemporary guidance.
Analyses are stratified by vascular territory and by event order, and the authors are explicit that the carotid result is underpowered rather than null.
Because Lp(a) is largely genetically determined and stable through life, confounding by lifestyle and reverse causation are less of a threat than for most biomarker-outcome associations.
limitations: Observational: association, not causation, although the genetic determination of Lp(a) mitigates this concern considerably.

Revascularization is a procedural rather than a hard biological outcome; it depends on symptom reporting, referral patterns, imaging access and operator thresholds, so it partly measures health-care behaviour rather than disease.

Restricted to UK Biobank participants of European ancestry, which excludes the groups with the highest Lp(a) levels (notably South Asian and African ancestry populations) and limits generalisability; UK Biobank participants are also healthier than the general population.
Lp(a) was measured once at baseline with an assay whose standardisation is not described, and no information is given on whether isoform-independent nmol/L measurement was used throughout.
The covariates included in adjustment are not reported in the abstract, so the extent to which the association is independent of LDL cholesterol, apoB and conventional risk factors cannot be judged.

The attenuation of the association from first to third procedure (HR 1.48, then 1.28, then 1.23 [0.94-1.62]) is at least partly explained by depletion of susceptibles and by the small numbers reaching three procedures, and should not be over-interpreted as biological.
Absolute risks are modest (4.36% vs 2.96% undergoing at least one procedure over 14 years), so the relative increase translates into a small absolute difference.
No data on whether lipid-lowering therapy modified the association; P values and funding are not reported.
42872886.practice_implications: This strengthens the case for measuring Lp(a) once in primary prevention: a level at or above 105 nmol/L marks patients who will accumulate roughly 50% more revascularization procedures over a decade and a half, across coronary and peripheral territories rather than coronary alone. Practically, a high Lp(a) should prompt more aggressive management of everything that is modifiable - LDL cholesterol to the lower end of target, blood pressure, smoking, antiplatelet consideration where otherwise indicated - and should raise the index of suspicion for peripheral as well as coronary disease on review. It does not establish that lowering Lp(a) reduces this burden; that awaits the ongoing outcome trials of targeted Lp(a)-lowering agents.

candidates.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of NT-proBNP thresholds in Dyspneic Patients in the Emergency Department according to patients' characteristics: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Concentrations of N-terminal pro-B type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is central to acute heart failure (AHF) diagnosis in dyspneic emergency departments (ED) patients, but optimal thresholds remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of various NT-proBNP thresholds for AHF, across the general population and these key subgroups.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted, including studies published up to August 28, 2025, that reported the diagnostic performance of NT-proBNP thresholds for AHF in dyspneic ED patients.
RESULTS: The analysis included 31 studies comprising 26,948 patients. To exclude AHF, a fixed threshold of ≤300 ng/L yielded an area under the receiver operator characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.73 (0.69-0.77), with high sensitivity of 97.9% (96.9-98.5) and lower specificity of 46.2% (36.4-56.2); the negative predictive value of this threshold was 97.0% (96.5-97.4). Age-dependent thresholds (≥450 ng/L for patients aged <50 years, ≥900 ng/L for those aged 50-75 years, and ≥1,800 ng/L for those aged ≥75 years), evaluated in 14,410 patients, achieved an AUC of 0.84 (0.83-0.85) with a more favorable balance between sensitivity of 85.9% (85.0-86.7) and specificity of 82.0% (81.2-82.9). In patients with CKD (N=2,271), all fixed thresholds yielded AUC <0.80; age-dependent thresholds showed an AUC of 0.77 (0.75-0.78) with specificity of 62.6% (59.4-65.7). In patients with obesity (body mass index ≥30), only age-dependent thresholds were assessed, in 3,562 patients; AUC was 0.82 (0.81-0.84) and sensitivity was 81.2% (79.2-83.1), broadly comparable to the overall population.
CONCLUSION: A threshold ≤300 ng/L provides excellent rule-out performance for AHF, while age-dependent NT-proBNP thresholds offer superior diagnostic performance for ruling in AHF in the ED compared to fixed thresholds, and demonstrate consistent accuracy across subgroups. However, evidence in patients with CKD and obesity remains limited, both in terms of sample size and the range of thresholds evaluated.

candidates.title: Risk-weighted apoB and lipoprotein-associated coronary risk across ethnic groups.
candidates.abstract:
AIMS: Apolipoprotein B (apoB) reflects the number of circulating atherogenic lipoproteins but does not account for differences in particle atherogenicity. Risk-weighted apoB (RW-apoB), which incorporates triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)), may better capture lipoprotein-driven coronary risk, but its performance across diverse populations remains uncertain. We assessed whether the prespecified triglyceride - and Lp(a)-weighted information captured by RW-apoB was associated with coronary events beyond apoB and compared the discrimination of RW-apoB and measured apoB across ethnicities.
METHODS: We analyzed 40,132 participants with 4,509 coronary events from ARIC, CARDIA, MESA, the Framingham Offspring Study, and China Kadoorie Biobank. RW-apoB was calculated using a prespecified equation. Mutually adjusted Cox estimates were pooled within ethnic groups using random-effects meta-analysis. Separate single-marker models compared discrimination. Sensitivity analyses included age and sex adjustment, standardized exposures, hard-events, truncated follow-up, and CKB-specific logistic regression.
RESULTS: Mean RW-apoB exceeded apoB by approximately 8 mg/dL in African American and Chinese participants, reflecting higher lipoprotein(a) and triglycerides, respectively. RW-apoB was associated with coronary events conditional on apoB in White, African American, Chinese, and Hispanic participants: hazard ratios per 10 mg/dL were 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.18), 1.11 (1.08-1.15), 1.08 (1.05-1.11), and 1.10 (1.01-1.21), respectively. C-indices for RW-apoB versus apoB were 0.630 versus 0.617 in White (P<0.001), 0.606 versus 0.595 in African American (P=0.085), 0.567 versus 0.554 in Chinese (P=0.014), and 0.540 versus 0.535 in Hispanic participants (P=0.756).
CONCLUSION: RW-apoB captured lipoprotein-associated risk beyond measured apoB, with discrimination gains statistically demonstrable in the larger White and Chinese groups.

candidates.title: Functional outcome after recurrent laryngeal nerve injury following thoracic aortic surgery.
candidates.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury is a recognized complication of aortic surgery, yet data on long-term functional outcomes remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and to assess voice recovery after thoracic aortic surgery.
METHODS: Single-centre retrospective analysis included adult patients undergoing aortic arch or thoracoabdominal aortic surgery between 2001 and 2024. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury was diagnosed by postoperative vocal cord paralysis. Aortic arch surgery included partial and total arch replacement, while thoracoabdominal surgery involved the proximal descending aorta. The primary endpoint was full voice recovery. Secondary endpoints included recovery of normal vocal cord mobility, residual dysphonia, the need for voice therapy, and vocal cord interventions.
RESULTS: Among 2,983 patients undergoing aortic surgery, 70 (2.3%) were diagnosed with postoperative recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Median follow-up was 17 [IQR: 7-25] months. The incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury was 1.7% after arch surgery and 5.3% after thoracoabdominal procedures. At final follow-up, 34 patients (50%) achieved full voice recovery, while 20 (30%) had mild dysphonia, 9 (13%) moderate dysphonia, and 5 (7%) severe dysphonia. Voice therapy was performed in 49 (70%) patients, and 10 (14%) required additional vocal cord interventions.
CONCLUSIONS: In this large cohort, the incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after aortic surgery was lower than previously reported. Functional outcomes were favourable, with most patients achieving full or near-complete voice recovery through conservative or interventional management. Structured follow-up and multidisciplinary care remain essential to optimize outcomes after recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
